corpus_definition: To be careful because of a possible danger.

forms.note: No noun is made from beware. Use 'care' or 'caution': 'Drive with caution.'

forms.definition: to be careful because something may be dangerous
forms.example: Beware of the dog when you open the gate.
forms.note: Used only in this base form: in orders and signs (Beware of pickpockets!) or after must/should/to. We don't say 'bewared' or 'bewaring'.

syn.note: Everyday spoken English: 'Watch out for the cars!'
Spoken, often a quick warning: 'Look out! The floor is wet.'
The easiest and most common way to say it.
Softer; often friendly advice, not a warning sign.
British English, in short warnings: 'Mind the step!'

ant.note: To pay no attention to a danger or a warning.

forms.note: No adjective is made from beware. 'Wary' (careful because you don't trust something) shares an old root 'ware' but is not made from beware.

context.text: There is a sign at the gate of my uncle's house in Fergana: 'Beware of the dog!' Guests should beware, because the dog is big and loud.

reviewer_note: Defective verb: only the base form is used; 'wary' kept as not_family, not a form.

corpus_definition: to offer a specific amount of money to buy something

forms.definition: an offer to pay a certain amount of money for something
forms.example: She made a high bid for the old carpet.

syn.note: Easy, general word with the same meaning.
Formal: a written offer from a company to do work for a price.

forms.definition: the act of people offering money for something at a sale
forms.example: The bidding started at one hundred dollars.

forms.definition: to offer a certain amount of money to buy something
forms.example: He bid 500 dollars for the painting at the auction.
forms.note: In this meaning the past tense and past participle are also 'bid': 'Yesterday she bid 200 dollars.'

syn.note: Easy word; bid is used especially at auctions.
Common phrase with the same meaning.
Related: when you bid you only offer money; you pay later if you win.

people.definition: a person who offers money for something at an auction
people.example: The highest bidder will take the car home.

context.text: At the auction in Tashkent, the bidding for an old carpet was very fast. My father bid 300 dollars, but another man made a higher bid and won it.

reviewer_note: Irregular past in the money sense (bid-bid-bid); other sense 'bid = try to get' (a bid for power) not included.

corpus_definition: To tie objects together using rope or string.

forms.definition: the cover that holds the pages of a book together
forms.example: This old book has a leather binding.
forms.note: Belongs to bind = fasten the pages of a book together, not tying things with rope.

forms.definition: to tie things together tightly with rope or string
forms.example: They used rope to bind the wood together.

syn.note: The easy, everyday word; bind is more formal or literary.
Common phrasal verb: 'tie up a parcel'.
More general: you can fasten with a rope, a button or a belt.
To cover something by putting paper or cloth around it, not always tightly.

ant.note: To open a knot and make things free again.
To let someone or something go free.

forms.definition: tied with rope so that it cannot move
forms.example: The thief was found with his hands bound behind his back.

syn.note: Easy word with the same meaning.
Common in spoken English.

forms.definition: that must be obeyed because it is part of an agreement or law
forms.example: The contract is legally binding.
forms.note: Belongs to bind = make someone do something by law or promise, not tying with rope.

people.definition: a hard cover with rings for keeping loose papers together
people.example: I keep my English notes in a blue binder.
people.note: Belongs to bind = hold papers together, not tying with rope.

context.text: After the harvest, my grandfather would bind the wheat with string. He carried the bound bundles to the cart one by one.

reviewer_note: bound kept as participial adjective (tied); legal 'binding' and folder 'binder' marked other_meaning.

corpus_definition: A strong and sudden explosion of energy or wind.

forms.definition: a sudden, strong explosion, or a strong rush of air
forms.example: The loud blast broke the nearby windows.

syn.note: The general word; blast often means the force of the explosion.
A short, loud noise; it is not always an explosion.
Only for wind: a sudden strong rush of air.
A short, sudden amount of something: a burst of energy.

forms.definition: to break or destroy rock or buildings with explosives
forms.example: Workers blasted a tunnel through the mountain.

syn.note: Everyday phrasal verb: 'blow up a bridge'.
Usually the bomb explodes by itself; you blast something with explosives.

context.text: Workers blasted the rock to build a new road near Chimgan. Every blast shook the windows of the houses in the village.

reviewer_note: Informal sense 'a blast = a very fun time' left out; the verb 'blast music' (play loudly) also not used.

particle_note: Separable: 'blow up the bridge' or 'blow the bridge up'; with a pronoun only 'blow it up'. Also used without an object: 'The car blew up.' Irregular: blow - blew - blown.

relations.note: To break or destroy with explosives; a little more technical.
Usually without an object: 'The bomb exploded.' Blow up is more common in speech.
General word: you can destroy something in many ways, not only with a bomb.
To stop a bomb from exploding by taking out a part of it.

context.text: In the film, the soldiers had to blow up the old bridge before the enemy arrived. When it blew up, the whole valley shook.

reviewer_note: Other meanings (fill with air: blow up a balloon; get very angry) left out.

corpus_definition: A close connection or strong feeling of friendship between people.

forms.definition: a strong feeling of friendship or love that connects people
forms.example: There is a strong bond between the two sisters.

syn.note: More general; can be any link, not always a warm feeling.
Often plural: 'family ties', 'close ties with Russia'.
A connection between people, places or things.
A relationship between friends; a bond can also be in a family.
The way two people are connected; it can be good or bad.

forms.definition: the process of people becoming close to each other
forms.example: The camping trip was good for team bonding.

forms.definition: to develop a close relationship with someone
forms.example: The new students bonded quickly during the trip.

syn.note: To feel that you understand someone: 'We really connected.'
Easy, everyday phrase.
To start a friendship; bond means the feeling becomes strong.

context.text: Ali bonded with his classmates during a school trip to Bukhara. Ten years later, the bond between them is still strong.

reviewer_note: Other senses of bond (money: government bond; chemistry) left out; 'bound' is not family here.

corpus_definition: Extra money given for doing a very good job.

forms.definition: extra money added to your pay for good work
forms.example: The staff received a holiday bonus.
forms.note: Also means any pleasant extra thing: 'The hotel was near the beach, which was a bonus.' Plural: bonuses.

syn.note: Something given for good work; it is not always money.
Simple phrase with the same idea.
Informal: an extra thing you get from your job, like a free phone.
Small money a customer gives a waiter or driver, not money from your boss.

context.text: My sister works at a bank in Tashkent. This year she got a big bonus because her team did very well, and she spent it on a trip to Samarkand.

reviewer_note: Single-word family; no forms in other slots.

corpus_definition: A line that marks the edge of an area.

forms.definition: a line that shows where one area ends and another starts
forms.example: The river forms a boundary between the two countries.
forms.note: Plural: boundaries. Also used for limits of behaviour: 'set boundaries'.

syn.note: Most often the line between two countries.
The border between countries, often in history or far areas.
The outside part of something, not always a line between two areas.
The furthest point you can go; often not a real line.
Very general word.

forms.definition: to form the edge of an area
forms.example: The farm is bounded by mountains in the north.
forms.note: Usually passive: 'be bounded by'. Not the past of bind.

syn.note: To be next to: 'Uzbekistan borders Kazakhstan.'
To be all around something.
To close an area in with a wall or fence.

forms.definition: without any end or limit
forms.example: Children seem to have boundless energy.
forms.note: Belongs to bound = limit, for energy or love, not a line on a map.

context.text: A small river forms the boundary between our farm and the neighbours' land. On the other side, the farm is bounded by a long wall.

reviewer_note: Verb bound (= form the edge of) is from the same root as boundary, not the past of bind; boundless kept as other_meaning (figurative limits).

corpus_definition: To talk too proudly about your own achievements.

forms.definition: talk in which someone is too proud of what they have done
forms.example: Everyone got tired of his bragging.

syn.note: Same meaning; a little more neutral.
Informal; can be about actions as well as words.

forms.definition: to talk too proudly about what you have or what you have done
forms.example: He likes to brag about his expensive car.
forms.note: brag about / of something; past: bragged.

syn.note: Same meaning; brag is a little more informal.
Informal; you can show off with actions, not only words.
Informal: to talk as if you are more important than you are.

people.definition: a person who often talks too proudly about themselves
people.example: Nobody likes a braggart at the dinner table.

context.text: My cousin likes to brag about his new phone. At dinner, everyone got bored of his bragging and changed the subject.

reviewer_note: braggart is old-fashioned but in learner dictionaries; no adjective/adverb exists.

corpus_definition: The quality of showing courage in dangerous situations.

forms.definition: the quality of not being afraid in danger
forms.example: The soldier was honored for his bravery.

syn.note: Same meaning and very common.
Very great courage, often to save other people.
Being confident and ready to take risks.
Literary, often about soldiers. American spelling: valor.

ant.note: Being too afraid to do what is right.

forms.definition: to face something difficult or dangerous without fear
forms.example: Hundreds of fans braved the cold to see the match.

syn.note: To deal with a difficult thing; less about courage.
To refuse to accept bad treatment from a person.
To refuse to obey, or to face danger in a strong way.

ant.note: To keep away from something difficult.

forms.definition: not afraid to do dangerous or difficult things
forms.example: It was very brave of you to jump into the river.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little more formal.
Not afraid at all.
Confident and ready to take risks.
Very brave, like a hero, often to help others.

ant.note: Too afraid to do the right thing.

forms.definition: in a way that shows no fear of danger
forms.example: She bravely spoke up against the unfair rule.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little more formal.
Without any fear at all.
In a confident way that takes risks.

context.text: A young firefighter in Namangan bravely carried a child out of a burning house. Everyone praised his bravery. 'He was so brave,' said the child's mother.

reviewer_note: bravery is made from brave (+ -ery, not in the affix table, so no affix claimed); verb brave = face danger.
